The big picture

An infinite series \sum a_j is not an infinite addition but a limit: we form the partial sums S_n = a_1 + \dots + a_n, a new sequence, and the series converges if (S_n) has a finite limit S, its sum; otherwise it diverges. So everything from 7 Limits of Sequences applies to (S_n), and the lecture turns those tools into tests that look only at the terms a_n. Two reference series anchor everything: the geometric series \sum q^j converges exactly for \lvert q\rvert < 1, and the harmonic series \sum \frac1j diverges although its terms tend to 0. That second fact shows that the term test (a_n \to 0) is necessary but never sufficient. The Cauchy criterion gives an exact test without knowing the sum; for non-negative terms convergence reduces to "partial sums bounded above", which gives the comparison test. Signs bring cancellation: Leibniz's test handles alternating series, and the split into absolute and conditional convergence decides whether the order of the terms matters (Riemann's rearrangement theorem). The ratio and root tests compare with a geometric series; Dirichlet's and Abel's tests handle oscillating factors.

Why series?

We know how to study a sequence of numbers. Now we ask what happens when we add its terms.

Start with a simple example:

\frac12 + \frac14 + \frac18 + \frac1{16} + \cdots

Successive sums:

\frac12,\ \frac34,\ \frac78,\ \frac{15}{16},\ \dots
Symbols
  • each fraction in the first line is a term being added: \frac{1}{2^j} for j = 1, 2, 3, \dots
  • each fraction in the second line is the total after adding the first 1, 2, 3, 4, \dots terms (the "successive sums", later called partial sums)

Picture on the slide ("Partial sums moving towards 1"): a bar from 0 to 1, filled up to \frac12, then \frac34, …

The sums approach 1 even though infinitely many positive terms are added.

Achilles and the tortoise

In Zeno's paradox, Achilles runs faster than a tortoise, but the tortoise has a head start. Each time Achilles reaches the tortoise's previous position, it has moved a little further.

Suppose: Achilles runs at 10 m/s, the tortoise at 1 m/s, and it starts 10 m ahead.

  • To cover the first 10 m, Achilles needs 1 s.
  • The tortoise has moved another 1 m: Achilles needs 0.1 s more.
  • Next he needs 0.01 s, then 0.001 s, and so on.
\text{Total time} = 1 + \frac1{10} + \frac1{100} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{10}\right)^k = \frac{10}{9}\ \text{s}.
Symbols
  • \left(\frac1{10}\right)^k — the time (s) Achilles needs for the (k+1)-th catch-up stage: each stage takes a tenth of the previous one, because the tortoise is 10 times slower
  • \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} — "add up the terms for k = 0, 1, 2, \dots"; defined below as a limit of partial sums
  • \frac{10}{9}\ \text{s} \approx 1.11 s — the total time, by the geometric-series formula of slide 11 with q = \frac1{10}

Schematic on the slide (not to scale): arrows for Achilles reaching the tortoise's previous position after 1 s, 0.1 s, 0.01 s, while the tortoise moves further.

Key message: Infinitely many terms do not necessarily mean an infinite sum.

Intuition — the paradox dissolves

Zeno's argument splits a finite time into infinitely many ever shorter pieces and then claims the pieces can never all be used up. The series says: the pieces add up to \frac{10}{9} s, and after that moment Achilles is ahead. Check without series: Achilles gains 10 - 1 = 9 m every second on a 10 m gap, so he closes it after \frac{10}{9} s. Same answer.

From a sequence to a series

Let (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} be a sequence of real numbers. The n-th partial sum is

S_n = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j.
S_1 = a_1, \qquad S_2 = a_1 + a_2, \qquad S_3 = a_1 + a_2 + a_3.
Symbols
  • a_j — the j-th term of the series (a real number)
  • S_n — the n-th partial sum: the ordinary finite sum of the first n terms
  • j — the summation index, a "dummy" variable: \sum_{j=1}^n a_j and \sum_{k=1}^n a_k mean the same

The partial sums (S_n) form another sequence.

Practice: Khan Academy – understanding series (linked on slide 4).

Definition of convergence of a series

The symbol \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j denotes the infinite series with terms a_j. It is convergent if its partial sums (S_n) converge to some S \in \mathbb{R}. In that case

\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j = S = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j.
Symbols
  • \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j — used for two things: the series itself (the "object" whose convergence we ask about) and, if it converges, its value
  • S \in \mathbb{R} — the sum of the series: the limit of the partial sums, in the sense of 7 Limits of Sequences › Definition of convergence

If (S_n) has no finite limit, the series is divergent.

The notation \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j is not ordinary finite addition: its value is defined through a limit.

Practice: Khan Academy – convergence and divergence of series (linked on slide 5).

Intuition — two sequences, never confuse them

Every series carries two sequences: the terms (a_n) (what you add at step n) and the partial sums (S_n) (the running total). "The series converges" is a statement about (S_n). Going back and forth: S_n = S_{n-1} + a_n, so a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} (with S_0 = 0). Writing \sum a_j = +\infty is common shorthand for "S_n \to +\infty" (7 Limits of Sequences › Infinite limits); such a series still counts as divergent.

Common mistake — "infinitely many positive terms must give \infty"

Tempting: every term adds something, so the total must grow without bound. But "grows" and "grows without bound" are different: S_n = 1 - 2^{-n} grows at every step and stays below 1. A positive series diverges only if the partial sums are unbounded (made precise in Series with non-negative terms). The opposite mistake is just as common: "terms go to 0, so the total is finite" — see The harmonic series.

Series in robotics and AI

Robotics: accumulated error. Suppose a robot's odometry overestimates each movement by 1 cm. After N movements, the accumulated position error is

E_N = \sum_{k=1}^{N} 0.01 = 0.01N\ \text{m}.
Symbols
  • E_N — total position error (m) after N movements; 0.01 m = 1 cm, the error added by each movement (always in the same direction: "systematic")

Even a small systematic error can grow without bound.

AI: discounted rewards. In reinforcement learning, future rewards are often discounted:

G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}, \qquad 0 < \gamma < 1.

If \lvert r_j\rvert \le R, then

\lvert G_t\rvert \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R = \frac{R}{1 - \gamma}.
Symbols
  • G_t — the return from time step t: the discounted total of all future rewards (dimensionless, or in "reward units")
  • r_{t+k+1} — the reward received k + 1 steps after time t
  • \gamma — the discount factor, 0 < \gamma < 1: a reward k steps later counts only \gamma^k as much
  • R — a bound on the size of every reward

Thus, the infinite sum has a finite value.

Key message: In robotics and AI, series describe accumulated quantities. Their convergence determines whether the total remains finite.

Unclear (slides 6, 50, 51)

The index of the reward is written three ways: G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k r_{t+k+1} (slide 6), G = \sum_n \gamma^n r_n starting at r_0 (slide 50) and G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k r_{t+k} (slide 51). Both r_{t+k+1} and r_{t+k} are in use in RL textbooks (they differ in whether the reward for the action at time t is called r_t or r_{t+1}); the bound \frac{R}{1-\gamma} is the same in every version. Not an error in the mathematics, just inconsistent notation.

Terms and partial sums are different

Example: a_n = 2^{-n} for n \ge 1.

Left: the terms a_n = 2^{-n} fall to 0. Right: the partial sums rise towards the dashed line at 1.

a_n \to 0, \qquad S_n = 1 - 2^{-n} \to 1.
Symbols
  • a_n = 2^{-n} = \frac{1}{2^n} — the terms; S_n = \sum_{j=1}^n 2^{-j} — the partial sums
  • the two limits are different numbers: the terms tend to 0, the sum is 1
Why is S_n = 1 - 2^{-n}?

Induction (1 Elements of Logic): S_1 = \frac12 = 1 - 2^{-1}. If S_n = 1 - 2^{-n}, then S_{n+1} = S_n + 2^{-(n+1)} = 1 - 2 \cdot 2^{-(n+1)} + 2^{-(n+1)} = 1 - 2^{-(n+1)}. In words: after each step the missing amount 1 - S_n = 2^{-n} halves, exactly like the robot's error in 7 Limits of Sequences › When is the robot close enough?.

The remainder after n terms

Suppose \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j converges to S. Its n-th remainder (or tail sum) is

r_n = S - S_n = \sum_{j=n+1}^{\infty} a_j.
S = \underbrace{a_1 + \dots + a_n}_{S_n} + \underbrace{a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} + \cdots}_{r_n}.
Symbols
  • S — the sum of the series; S_n — its n-th partial sum
  • r_n — the remainder: everything not yet added after n terms; the error made by using S_n in place of S
  • (this r_n is unrelated to the rewards r_n of the RL example)

For a convergent series r_n \to 0. The remainder is not automatically a finite real number for a divergent series.

Intuition

r_n \to 0 is just "S_n \to S" rewritten: r_n = S - S_n. The remainder is what numerical work cares about: "how many terms do I need for 3 correct decimals?" means "when is \lvert r_n\rvert < 0.0005?" — the question answered for alternating series by Leibniz's error bound below.

An example: \sum 1/j^2 converges

Task: Show that \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{j^2} converges, without calculating its sum.

Recall from Limits: a sequence converges in \mathbb{R} if and only if it satisfies the Cauchy criterion (7 Limits of Sequences › The Cauchy convergence criterion). For j \ge 2,

0 < \frac{1}{j^2} < \frac{1}{j(j-1)} = \frac{1}{j-1} - \frac1j.

For m > n \ge 1,

0 < S_m - S_n = \sum_{j=n+1}^{m} \frac{1}{j^2} < \sum_{j=n+1}^{m} \left(\frac{1}{j-1} - \frac1j\right) = \frac1n - \frac1m \le \frac1n.
Symbols
  • S_n = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac1{j^2} — the partial sums; m > n — two indices, S_m - S_n the sum of the terms with index n+1, \dots, m
  • \frac{1}{j-1} - \frac1j — a telescoping term: in the sum, consecutive pieces cancel

Thus (S_n) is a Cauchy sequence and the series converges.

Why does the telescoping sum collapse to \frac1n - \frac1m, and why does \frac1n finish the proof?

Write out the sum: \left(\frac1n - \frac1{n+1}\right) + \left(\frac1{n+1} - \frac1{n+2}\right) + \dots + \left(\frac1{m-1} - \frac1m\right). Every inner fraction appears once with + and once with -, so only the first and last survive. (Partial fraction check: \frac{1}{j-1} - \frac1j = \frac{j - (j-1)}{j(j-1)} = \frac{1}{j(j-1)}.) For the Cauchy criterion: given \varepsilon > 0, choose N > \frac1\varepsilon. For m > n \ge N: \lvert S_m - S_n\rvert < \frac1n \le \frac1N < \varepsilon. The bound \frac1n does not depend on m, and that is exactly what "Cauchy" needs. (The sum is in fact \frac{\pi^2}{6} \approx 1.645, but finding that needs tools far beyond this lecture; the point here is convergence without knowing the value.)

Geometric series

For q \in \mathbb{R}, the geometric series is

\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} q^j = 1 + q + q^2 + \cdots.

Its partial sum is S_n = 1 + q + \dots + q^n. Subtract qS_n from S_n:

(1 - q)S_n = 1 - q^{n+1}.

If q \neq 1,

S_n = \frac{1 - q^{n+1}}{1 - q}.
Symbols
  • q — the ratio: each term is q times the previous one; the first term is q^0 = 1
  • S_n — here the sum of the n + 1 terms q^0, \dots, q^n (the series starts at j = 0, so the count is shifted by one)
  • q^{n+1} — the first power not included
Why does subtracting qS_n work?

S_n = 1 + q + q^2 + \dots + q^n and qS_n = q + q^2 + \dots + q^n + q^{n+1}. Every power from q to q^n appears in both, so the difference is S_n - qS_n = 1 - q^{n+1}. Dividing by 1 - q needs q \neq 1; for q = 1 every term is 1 and S_n = n + 1. Check: q = \frac12, n = 5: 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1{32} = \frac{63}{32} and \frac{1 - (1/2)^6}{1/2} = \frac{63}{32}.

When does a geometric series converge?

For \lvert q\rvert < 1, we have q^{n+1} \to 0. Therefore

\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} q^j = \frac{1}{1 - q} \qquad \text{if } \lvert q\rvert < 1.
Symbols
  • q — the ratio, with \lvert q\rvert < 1; q^{n+1} \to 0 by 7 Limits of Sequences › Powers
  • \frac{1}{1-q} — the sum: the limit of S_n = \frac{1 - q^{n+1}}{1-q}

For q = 1, the partial sums grow without bound. For q = -1, they alternate between 1 and 0. For \lvert q\rvert > 1, the terms q^n do not tend to zero. In all these cases the series diverges.

Practice: Khan Academy – geometric series of constants (linked on slide 11).

Worked example — a geometric series that doesn't start at 1

Find \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} 3\left(-\frac25\right)^n.

  1. Identify the ratio: each term is -\frac25 times the previous one, so q = -\frac25; \lvert q\rvert < 1, so it converges.
  2. Factor out the first term (n = 2): 3 \cdot \left(-\frac25\right)^2 = \frac{12}{25}, and the rest is \frac{12}{25}\left(1 + q + q^2 + \cdots\right).
  3. Apply the formula: \frac{12}{25} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - (-2/5)} = \frac{12}{25} \cdot \frac57 = \frac{12}{35} \approx 0.343. Rule to remember: sum = first term /\,(1 - \text{ratio}), whatever the starting index.

Repeating decimals are geometric series: 0.\overline{36} = \frac{36}{100} + \frac{36}{100^2} + \cdots = \frac{36/100}{1 - 1/100} = \frac{36}{99} = \frac{4}{11}.

Common mistake — using \frac{1}{1-q} for every geometric series

\frac{1}{1-q} is the sum only when the series starts with the term 1 (j = 0). \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac1{2^j} starts with \frac12, so its sum is \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1, not \frac{1}{1 - 1/2} = 2. And the formula is only valid for \lvert q\rvert < 1: plugging q = 2 into \frac{1}{1-q} gives -1, which is nonsense for a sum of positive terms that diverges.

Adding halves

\frac12 + \frac14 + \frac18 + \cdots = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^j} = 1.
Symbols
  • the geometric series with first term \frac12 and ratio \frac12; sum \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1

Picture on the slide: the interval [0, 1] is filled by consecutive pieces of length \frac12, \frac14, \frac18, \dots

Each step covers half of what remains. The total approaches 1 without ever exceeding it.

Filling a square

The same series, as areas:

A unit square cut into rectangles of area \frac12, \frac14, \frac18, \frac1{16}, \dots; each new piece is half of the part not yet covered.

Key message: Infinitely many positive terms may have a finite sum.

The harmonic series

The harmonic series \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \frac1j is divergent.

Group the terms:

\underbrace{1}_{1} + \underbrace{\frac12}_{\frac12} + \underbrace{\left(\frac13 + \frac14\right)}_{\ge \frac12} + \underbrace{\left(\frac15 + \dots + \frac18\right)}_{\ge \frac12} + \cdots

Every new group has twice as many terms, each at least as large as its final term. Hence

S_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac{k}{2} \xrightarrow{k \to \infty} +\infty.
Symbols
  • S_{2^k} — the partial sum up to the term \frac{1}{2^k}: it contains the first term 1, the single term \frac12, and k - 1 further groups
  • each group runs from \frac{1}{2^{i-1}+1} to \frac{1}{2^i}: 2^{i-1} terms, each \ge \frac{1}{2^i}, so the group is \ge \frac12
Why is the whole sequence (S_n) unbounded, not just the subsequence S_{2^k}?

The terms are positive, so (S_n) is increasing: for any n \ge 2^k, S_n \ge S_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac k2. Given any bound M, choose k > 2M; then all S_n with n \ge 2^k exceed M, so S_n \to +\infty. It is very slow: 1 + \frac k2 only passes 10 at k = 19, i.e. after about half a million terms. (Its second proof, via the Cauchy criterion, is below; the same estimate appeared in 7 Limits of Sequences › Why neighbouring terms are not enough.)

Smaller terms do not guarantee convergence

Harmonic series \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1nSquare-reciprocal series \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}
diverges — its partial sums grow without boundconverges — its partial sums satisfy the Cauchy criterion

In both cases, a_n \to 0. The behaviour of the partial sums is what matters.

Intuition — how fast the terms shrink

\frac1n and \frac1{n^2} both shrink to 0, but \frac1n shrinks so slowly that the blocks "\frac1{n+1} + \dots + \frac1{2n}" never get small: n terms of size about \frac1{2n} always add to about \frac12. For \frac1{n^2} the same block has n terms of size about \frac1{4n^2}, totalling about \frac1{4n} \to 0. Convergence is a contest between how many terms are left and how small they are.

Adding and scaling convergent series

If \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n and \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n converge and c, d \in \mathbb{R}, then

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (c a_n + d b_n) = c \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n + d \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n.

Why? The corresponding partial sums satisfy

\sum_{n=1}^{N} (c a_n + d b_n) = c \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n + d \sum_{n=1}^{N} b_n.

Now take N \to \infty and use the limit laws for sequences (7 Limits of Sequences › Arithmetic of finite limits).

Symbols
  • c, d — fixed real constants; N — the number of terms in the finite partial sums
  • the finite equation holds by ordinary rules of addition (reorder and factor out constants in a finite sum)
Common mistake — splitting a sum that doesn't converge

The rule needs both series to converge. \sum (1 - 1) = 0 converges, but writing it as \sum 1 - \sum 1 produces "\infty - \infty", an indeterminate form (7 Limits of Sequences › Indeterminate forms are warnings). Likewise there is no product rule "\sum a_n b_n = \left(\sum a_n\right)\left(\sum b_n\right)" — see Operations with absolutely convergent series.

Changing a finite number of terms

Adding, deleting, or changing finitely many terms does not change whether a series converges. It can change the sum.

For m \in \mathbb{N}, the series \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j converges if and only if its tail \sum_{j=m+1}^{\infty} a_j converges.

\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} a_j = \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{m} a_j}_{\text{finite}} + \sum_{j=m+1}^{\infty} a_j.
Symbols
  • m — a fixed number of initial terms; \sum_{j=1}^m a_j — an ordinary finite sum (a fixed real number)
  • \sum_{j=m+1}^{\infty} a_j — the tail starting at index m + 1

The tail sum is the remainder r_m when the original series converges.

Connection

This is the series version of 7 Limits of Sequences › Changing a finite number of terms: the partial sums of the tail are S_n - S_m (n > m), which differ from S_n by a constant, so one converges iff the other does. Practical consequence: every convergence test only needs its hypothesis from some index N on — the slides' comparison and ratio tests say "\forall n \ge N" for exactly this reason.

A necessary condition for convergence

Theorem (Necessary condition for convergence of a series). If the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges, then

\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0.

Proof: Let S_n = \sum_{j=1}^n a_j, and suppose S_n \to S \in \mathbb{R}. Then also S_{n-1} \to S, and

a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \longrightarrow S - S = 0.
Symbols
  • S_{n-1} — the partial sums shifted by one index: the same sequence with its first term dropped, so it has the same limit (7 Limits of Sequences › Properties of subsequences)
  • a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} — the n-th term is the step between consecutive partial sums

The condition a_n \to 0 is not sufficient

If a_n \not\to 0, the series must diverge. But if a_n \to 0, we still need another argument.

ConvergesDiverges
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}, \ \frac{1}{n^2} \to 0\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1n, \ \frac1n \to 0 as well

Term test: useful for proving divergence, not convergence.

Worked example — the term test

(a) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{2n+1}. Check the terms: \frac{n}{2n+1} = \frac{1}{2 + 1/n} \to \frac12 \neq 0. Conclude: the series diverges (the partial sums grow by about \frac12 per step). (b) \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n. Check the terms: (-1)^n has no limit, so certainly a_n \not\to 0. Conclude: divergent (partial sums -1, 0, -1, 0, \dots). (c) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}. Check the terms: \to 0. Conclude: no conclusion from the term test; another test is needed (comparison with \frac{1}{n^2} shows convergence, see Comparison test for non-negative series).

Common mistake — "the terms tend to 0, so the series converges"

This is the single most frequent error with series. The theorem is an implication "converges ⇒ a_n \to 0"; its converse is false, and the harmonic series is the counterexample. Only the contrapositive is valid: "a_n \not\to 0 ⇒ diverges" (1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive). So when a_n \to 0, write "the term test is inconclusive", never "converges".

The Cauchy criterion for series

Theorem (Cauchy convergence criterium). The series \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges if and only if

\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N \in \mathbb{N}\ \ \forall n \ge N\ \ \forall p \in \mathbb{N}_0 : \quad \left\lvert \sum_{j=n}^{n+p} a_j \right\rvert < \varepsilon.
Symbols
  • n — where a block of terms starts (from N on); p \in \mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} — how many further terms the block has, so the block is a_n, \dots, a_{n+p} (p + 1 terms)
  • \left\lvert \sum_{j=n}^{n+p} a_j \right\rvert — the absolute value of the block sum
  • \varepsilon, N — tolerance and starting index, as in 7 Limits of Sequences › Definition of a Cauchy sequence

Meaning: Every sufficiently late block of consecutive terms has a sum whose absolute value is small, no matter how long the block is.

This is the Cauchy criterion for the partial sums, since \sum_{j=n}^{n+p} a_j = S_{n+p} - S_{n-1}.

Unclear (slide 20)

The theorem is titled "Cauchy convergence criterium" on the slide (transcribed as printed); the usual English is "criterion". Spelling only.

Intuition

Why it matters: the definition of convergence needs the sum S, which we usually don't know. The Cauchy criterion only asks about the terms. Taking the block of length one (p = 0) gives \lvert a_n\rvert < \varepsilon, i.e. a_n \to 0: the term test is the special case "blocks of length 1". The harmonic series passes that special case and fails for long blocks — next slide. (The convention S_0 = 0 makes the formula S_{n+p} - S_{n-1} work for n = 1 too.)

The harmonic series fails the Cauchy criterion

Consider the block from n to 2n - 1:

\sum_{j=n}^{2n-1} \frac1j \ge \underbrace{\frac{1}{2n} + \dots + \frac{1}{2n}}_{n \text{ terms}} = \frac12.
Symbols
  • the block \frac1n + \frac1{n+1} + \dots + \frac1{2n-1} has n terms, each at least \frac{1}{2n} (the smallest of them, \frac1{2n-1}, is still larger than \frac1{2n})
  • in the criterion's notation: start n, length parameter p = n - 1

These blocks occur arbitrarily far along the sequence, but their sums do not become smaller than \frac12.

Thus the harmonic series is not Cauchy, so it diverges.

How exactly does this violate the criterion?

The criterion's negation (1 Elements of Logic): \exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n \ge N\ \exists p \in \mathbb{N}_0 : \left\lvert \sum_{j=n}^{n+p} a_j\right\rvert \ge \varepsilon. Take \varepsilon = \frac12. For any N, choose n = N and p = N - 1: the block from N to 2N - 1 has sum \ge \frac12. So no N works, and the criterion fails.

Series with non-negative terms

Suppose a_n \ge 0 for every n \in \mathbb{N}. Then

S_{n+1} - S_n = a_{n+1} \ge 0.

The partial sums (S_n) are non-decreasing. Therefore:

Lemma. For a series with non-negative terms, the following properties hold:

  • \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges \iff (S_n) is bounded above.
  • If the series converges, its sum is
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n = \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} S_n.
Symbols
  • S_n — the partial sums, non-decreasing because each step adds a_{n+1} \ge 0
  • \sup_{n} S_n — the supremum of all partial sums (3 Set of Real Numbers)
Connection

This is the monotone convergence theorem (7 Limits of Sequences › The monotone convergence theorem, also recapped in the pre-tutorial 6 notes as "a non-decreasing real sequence bounded above converges to its supremum") applied to (S_n). Conversely, "converges ⇒ bounded" is 7 Limits of Sequences › Convergence and boundedness. So for non-negative series there are only two outcomes: a finite sum, or S_n \to +\infty (7 Limits of Sequences › Monotone but not bounded?). Oscillation is impossible.

A useful subsequence criterion

Lemma. For a series with a_n \ge 0, convergence of one subsequence (S_{n_k}) of its partial sums already implies convergence of the whole series.

Reason: A convergent subsequence is bounded above, say S_{n_k} \le M. For every n, choose k with n_k \ge n. Because (S_n) is non-decreasing,

S_n \le S_{n_k} \le M.

The complete sequence (S_n) is bounded above, hence convergent.

Symbols
  • (S_{n_k}) — a subsequence of the partial sums (7 Limits of Sequences › Subsequences), e.g. S_2, S_4, S_8, \dots
  • M — an upper bound for the subsequence; k — chosen so that n_k \ge n (possible because n_k \to \infty)
Common mistake — dropping "a_n \ge 0"

For signed terms the lemma is false: for \sum (-1)^{n} the subsequence S_{2k} = 0 converges, but (S_n) = -1, 0, -1, 0, \dots does not. Monotonicity of (S_n) is what lets one good subsequence control everything; without it, a subsequence says nothing about the rest.

Comparison test for non-negative series

Theorem (Comparison convergence test). Suppose there exists N \in \mathbb{N} such that

0 \le a_n \le b_n \qquad \forall n \ge N.

Then:

  • If \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n converges, then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges.
  • If \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n diverges, then \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n diverges.
Symbols
  • (a_n) — the smaller, (b_n) — the larger non-negative sequence (from index N on)
  • \sum b_n — the "majorant" (used to prove convergence); \sum a_n — the "minorant" (used to prove divergence)

The second implication is the contrapositive of the first.

Why does the comparison test hold?

By Changing a finite number of terms we may start both series at N. Write A_n, B_n for the partial sums from N to n. Then 0 \le A_n \le B_n \le \sum_{j=N}^\infty b_j =: B, because (B_n) is non-decreasing and converges to its supremum B. So (A_n) is bounded above, hence converges by the lemma on Series with non-negative terms. The second statement is the contrapositive (1 Elements of Logic › Proof by contrapositive).

Comparison test: an example

Does the series converge for every \alpha \in \mathbb{R}?

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sin^2(n\alpha)}{2^n}

Since 0 \le \sin^2(n\alpha) \le 1,

0 \le \frac{\sin^2(n\alpha)}{2^n} \le \frac{1}{2^n}.

Because \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n} = 1, the given series converges for every \alpha \in \mathbb{R}.

Symbols
  • \alpha — a fixed real parameter; \sin^2(n\alpha) = (\sin(n\alpha))^2, always between 0 and 1
  • \frac{1}{2^n} — the convergent majorant (geometric series with ratio \frac12)
Worked example — choosing the comparison series

(a) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2 + n + 1}. Guess: for large n the term behaves like \frac1{n^2}, which converges, so look for an upper bound. Bound: n^2 + n + 1 > n^2, so 0 < \frac{1}{n^2 + n + 1} < \frac{1}{n^2}. Conclude: converges, since \sum \frac1{n^2} converges (An example: \sum 1/j^2 converges). (b) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n+1}{n^2}. Guess: behaves like \frac1n, which diverges, so look for a lower bound. Bound: \frac{n+1}{n^2} \ge \frac{n}{n^2} = \frac1n \ge 0. Conclude: diverges, since \sum \frac1n diverges. Direction check: to prove convergence, bound from above by a convergent series; to prove divergence, bound from below by a divergent one. The other two combinations prove nothing: \frac{1}{n^2} \le \frac1n does not tell you anything about \sum\frac{1}{n^2}.

Alternating series

An alternating series has terms that alternate in sign, for example

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n-1} b_n = b_1 - b_2 + b_3 - b_4 + \cdots, \qquad b_n \ge 0.
Symbols
  • b_n \ge 0 — the sizes of the terms; (-1)^{n-1} — the sign: + for odd n, - for even n

Example:

1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \frac14 + \cdots
Symbols
  • here b_n = \frac1n: the alternating harmonic series

It is not enough that signs alternate: the sizes of the terms determine convergence.

Leibniz's alternating-series test

Theorem (Leibniz convergence test). Let (b_n) be non-increasing, with b_n \ge 0 and b_n \to 0. Then

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n-1} b_n \quad \text{converges.}

If its sum is S, then

\lvert S - S_n\rvert \le b_{n+1}.
Symbols
  • S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k-1} b_k — the n-th partial sum; S — the sum
  • \lvert S - S_n\rvert — the error after n terms (the size of the remainder r_n)
  • b_{n+1} — the size of the first omitted term

The error after n terms is no larger than the magnitude of the first omitted term.

Practice: Khan Academy – alternating series (linked on slide 27).

Leibniz's test: alternating harmonic series

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n} = 1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \cdots

Here b_n = 1/n is positive, decreases, and tends to 0. Therefore the series converges, although \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1n diverges.

Error estimate: For its partial sums,

\lvert S - S_n\rvert \le \frac{1}{n+1}.

For error below 0.01, it is enough to take n \ge 100.

Symbols
  • S — the sum of the alternating harmonic series (= \ln 2 \approx 0.693, stated on slide 36); S_n — its partial sums
  • \frac1{n+1} = b_{n+1} — the bound from Leibniz's test; \frac1{101} < 0.01, while n = 99 only gives \frac1{100} = 0.01

(Checked numerically: the actual error at n = 100 is about 0.005, half the bound — the bound is safe, not sharp.)

Why Leibniz's test works

For b_n \ge b_{n+1} \ge 0, the partial sums alternate around their limit.

S_2 \le S_4 \le S_6 \le \cdots, \qquad S_1 \ge S_3 \ge S_5 \ge \cdots.
S_{2k+1} - S_{2k} = b_{2k+1} \to 0.
Symbols
  • S_{2k} — the even partial sums (end on a subtracted term): the lower sequence
  • S_{2k+1} — the odd partial sums (end on an added term): the upper sequence
  • b_{2k+1} — the gap between them: the one term that the odd sum has in addition

The lower and upper partial sums get closer together.

Partial sums of 1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \cdots: odd sums (blue) fall, even sums (orange) rise, both towards the dashed level S.

Since b_n \to 0, both subsequences approach the same limit.

Why are the even sums increasing, the odd sums decreasing, and why the error bound?

Monotone: S_{2k+2} - S_{2k} = b_{2k+1} - b_{2k+2} \ge 0 and S_{2k+3} - S_{2k+1} = -b_{2k+2} + b_{2k+3} \le 0, both because (b_n) is non-increasing. Bounded: S_{2k} \le S_{2k+1} \le S_1, so the even sums are bounded above by S_1; likewise the odd sums are bounded below by S_2. Same limit: both converge by monotone convergence; their difference b_{2k+1} \to 0, so the limits agree, say S. Every term is in one of the two subsequences, so S_n \to S. Error bound: S lies between any two consecutive partial sums (above every even one, below every odd one). So \lvert S - S_n\rvert \le \lvert S_{n+1} - S_n\rvert = b_{n+1}.

Worked example — Leibniz with an error target

\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{\sqrt n}: converge? how many terms for error < 0.1?

  1. Identify b_n: b_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt n} \ge 0.
  2. Check the three conditions: non-increasing (\sqrt{n+1} > \sqrt n), and \frac1{\sqrt n} \to 0. So the series converges by Leibniz.
  3. Error bound: \lvert S - S_n\rvert \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}} < 0.1 \iff \sqrt{n+1} > 10 \iff n + 1 > 100, so n \ge 100 terms suffice.
  4. Absolutely? \sum \frac{1}{\sqrt n} \ge \sum \frac1n termwise, which diverges, so the convergence is only conditional (next section).
Common mistake — forgetting "non-increasing"

Alternating signs plus b_n \to 0 is not enough; Leibniz needs (b_n) to be non-increasing (from some index on). Without it the cancellation can be unbalanced: if the positive terms are \frac1n-sized and the negative ones \frac1{n^2}-sized, the positive part wins and the partial sums run off to +\infty, although the signs alternate and the terms tend to 0. Check all three conditions every time.

Absolute and conditional convergence

A series \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n is absolutely convergent if \sum_{n=1}^\infty \lvert a_n\rvert converges.

It is conditionally convergent if \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges but \sum_{n=1}^\infty \lvert a_n\rvert diverges.

Examples:

  • \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} converges absolutely.
  • \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n} converges conditionally.
Intuition

Absolute convergence means the series would converge even if every sign were turned to +: the terms are small enough on their own, cancellation is not needed. Conditional convergence means the series survives only because of cancellation between positive and negative terms. The rest of the lecture shows that this difference decides whether reordering is safe.

Absolute convergence implies convergence

Theorem. If \sum_{n=1}^\infty \lvert a_n\rvert converges, then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges.

Proof using the Cauchy criterion: For all m \ge n,

\left\lvert \sum_{j=n}^{m} a_j \right\rvert \le \sum_{j=n}^{m} \lvert a_j\rvert.

Because \sum_{n=1}^\infty \lvert a_j\rvert is Cauchy, the right-hand side becomes arbitrarily small for all sufficiently large n, independently of m. Therefore \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_j is Cauchy and converges.

Symbols
  • the inequality is the triangle inequality for finitely many numbers, \lvert x_1 + \dots + x_k\rvert \le \lvert x_1\rvert + \dots + \lvert x_k\rvert (3 Set of Real Numbers)
  • "Cauchy" — the The Cauchy criterion for series, with m = n + p
Common mistake — reading the theorem backwards

"Converges ⇒ converges absolutely" is false: the alternating harmonic series converges, \sum \frac1n does not. The useful strategy is in the theorem's direction: test \sum\lvert a_n\rvert first (it has non-negative terms, so comparison, ratio and root tests apply); if it converges, you are done. Only if it diverges do you need Leibniz, Dirichlet or Abel.

Operations with absolutely convergent series

Suppose \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n and \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n converge absolutely.

  • For c, d \in \mathbb{R}, the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty (c a_n + d b_n) converges absolutely.
  • Their Cauchy product also converges absolutely. With
c_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k b_{n+1-k},

we have

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_n = \left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\right) \left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\right).
Symbols
  • c_n — the n-th term of the Cauchy product: the sum of all products a_k b_l whose indices add up to k + l = n + 1 (here c_n is a new sequence, unrelated to the constant c in the first bullet)
  • c_1 = a_1 b_1, c_2 = a_1 b_2 + a_2 b_1, c_3 = a_1 b_3 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_1

The product of two series is not generally obtained by multiplying corresponding terms.

Worked example — squaring a geometric series

Take a_n = b_n = q^{n-1} with \lvert q\rvert < 1, so both series are 1 + q + q^2 + \dots = \frac{1}{1-q}, absolutely convergent.

  1. Form the Cauchy product: c_n = \sum_{k=1}^n q^{k-1} q^{n-k} = \sum_{k=1}^n q^{n-1} = n\,q^{n-1} (n equal terms).
  2. Apply the theorem: \sum_{n=1}^\infty n\,q^{n-1} = \frac{1}{(1-q)^2}.
  3. Check with q = \frac12: 1 + 2 \cdot \frac12 + 3 \cdot \frac14 + 4 \cdot \frac18 + \dots = \frac{1}{(1/2)^2} = 4 (numerically confirmed). Multiplying "corresponding terms" would instead give \sum q^{2(n-1)} = \frac{1}{1 - q^2} = \frac43 for q = \frac12 — a different number.

Rearranging the terms of a series

A rearrangement changes the order of the terms, but uses each term exactly once. For example, it may be written as \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{\pi(n)}, where \pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} is a bijection.

Symbols
  • \pi — a bijection of \mathbb{N} (5 Functions › Injective, surjective, bijective): "the n-th term of the new series is the \pi(n)-th term of the old one"; bijective = every old term is used, and none twice

For a finite sum, changing the order never changes its value. For an infinite series, the answer can depend on the type of convergence.

\text{absolute convergence} \iff \text{every rearrangement has the same finite sum.}
Symbols
  • "every rearrangement has the same finite sum" — for every bijection \pi, \sum a_{\pi(n)} converges, to the same value as \sum a_n

This property is also called unconditional convergence. For a conditionally convergent real series, rearrangement can change the sum.

Intuition — why order can matter at all

A rearranged series has different partial sums: S_{10} of the new series adds a different set of ten terms. The sum is the limit of those partial sums, so there is no reason in general for it to be the same. Absolute convergence rescues the situation: the total "mass" \sum\lvert a_n\rvert is finite, so far-out terms carry almost nothing, whatever the order.

Conditional convergence: positive and negative parts

Write a_n = a_n^+ + a_n^-, where

a_n^+ = \max\{a_n, 0\}, \qquad a_n^- = \min\{a_n, 0\}.
Symbols
  • a_n^+ \ge 0 — the positive part: a_n if positive, otherwise 0
  • a_n^- \le 0 — the negative part: a_n if negative, otherwise 0 (in this lecture's convention it keeps its sign; some books define it as \max\{-a_n, 0\} \ge 0 instead)

Lemma. If \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges conditionally, then

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n^+ = +\infty, \qquad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n^- = -\infty.
Symbols
  • "= +\infty" — the partial sums tend to +\infty (the series diverges to +\infty)

The positive and negative contributions are both unbounded in magnitude; their interleaving produces the finite sum.

Why must both parts diverge?

Note a_n^+ = \frac{a_n + \lvert a_n\rvert}{2} and a_n^- = \frac{a_n - \lvert a_n\rvert}{2}. If \sum a_n^+ converged, then \sum a_n^- = \sum (a_n - a_n^+) would converge too (difference of convergent series), and so would \sum \lvert a_n\rvert = \sum (a_n^+ - a_n^-) — contradicting "conditional". The same argument rules out a convergent \sum a_n^-. Since these are series of one sign, "not convergent" means \pm\infty (Series with non-negative terms).

Riemann's rearrangement theorem

Theorem (Riemann series theorem). If a real series converges conditionally, then for every A \in \mathbb{R} there is a rearrangement of its terms whose partial sums converge to A.

Idea: Take positive terms until the sum passes A, then negative terms until it falls below A, and repeat. As the individual terms tend to 0, the overshoots and undershoots shrink.

The theorem is about changing the order of infinitely many terms, not changing finitely many.

Intuition

The lemma above is the fuel: since the positive terms alone add up to +\infty, there is always enough positive "supply" left to climb above A again, however far down the sum went; likewise for the negative terms. And since a_n \to 0 (the series converges), each crossing overshoots A by at most the last term used, which shrinks to 0. The same recipe can even make the partial sums tend to +\infty.

Rearrangement changes the partial sums

Consider the alternating harmonic series and the rearrangement that takes one positive term, then two negative terms.

Original order:

1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \frac14 + \cdots

New order:

1 - \frac12 - \frac14 + \frac13 - \frac16 - \frac18 + \cdots
Symbols
  • the new order uses the odd reciprocals 1, \frac13, \frac15, \dots once each with +, and the even reciprocals \frac12, \frac14, \frac16, \dots once each with -, two of them after every positive term

Same terms; different partial sums.

Partial sums of the original order (blue dots, levelling at \ln 2 \approx 0.69) and of the rearranged order (orange squares, levelling at \frac12\ln 2 \approx 0.35).

The original sum is \ln 2. The rearranged sum is \frac12 \ln 2.

Why is the rearranged sum exactly half?

Group the new order in blocks of three, \left(\frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{4k-2}\right) - \frac{1}{4k}, and note \frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{4k-2} = \frac{1}{4k-2}. So each block is \frac{1}{4k-2} - \frac{1}{4k} = \frac12\left(\frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{2k}\right), which is half of the k-th pair of the original series. Adding the blocks: the partial sums after 3k terms are half the original partial sums after 2k terms, which tend to \frac12 \ln 2; the partial sums in between differ from these by single terms \to 0. (Numerically: 600 000 rearranged terms give 0.346573 against \frac12\ln 2 = 0.346574.) That 1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \dots = \ln 2 is stated on the slide; its proof needs Taylor series, later in the course.

Common mistake — "a sum doesn't depend on the order"

True for finite sums (commutativity) and for absolutely convergent series — but not for conditionally convergent ones, as this example shows. Practically: never regroup or reorder the terms of a series unless you know it converges absolutely. (Inserting brackets without reordering is harmless for a convergent series: it just picks a subsequence of the partial sums.)

Comparison test for absolute convergence

Theorem (Comparison convergence test). Suppose there exists N \in \mathbb{N} such that

0 \le c_n \le \lvert a_n\rvert \le b_n \qquad \forall n \ge N.

Then:

  • If \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n converges, then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges absolutely.
  • If \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n diverges, then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n does not converge absolutely.
Symbols
  • (a_n) — the series under study, with any signs; \lvert a_n\rvert — the sizes of its terms
  • (b_n) — a non-negative upper comparison sequence; (c_n) — a non-negative lower comparison sequence

In the second case, the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n may still converge conditionally.

Connection

This is the earlier Comparison test for non-negative series applied to \sum \lvert a_n\rvert, combined with Absolute convergence implies convergence. Example: \left\lvert \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\right\rvert \le \frac{1}{n^2} gives absolute convergence; \left\lvert\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}\right\rvert \ge \frac1n only rules out absolute convergence, and Leibniz then shows conditional convergence.

Ratio test

Ratio test: a geometric bound

Assume a_n \neq 0 for all sufficiently large n.

Absolute convergence. If there exist L < 1 and N such that

\left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert \le L \qquad (n \ge N),

then \sum a_n converges absolutely. Indeed, \lvert a_n\rvert \le \lvert a_N\rvert L^{n-N} for n \ge N.

Divergence. If, for some N,

\left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert \ge 1 \qquad (n \ge N),

then \sum a_n diverges. Indeed, \lvert a_n\rvert \ge \lvert a_N\rvert > 0, so a_n \not\to 0.

Symbols
  • \left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right\rvert — the factor by which the size of the terms changes from index n to n + 1
  • L — one fixed number with 0 \le L < 1 that bounds all these factors from N on
  • \lvert a_N\rvert L^{n-N} — a geometric sequence with ratio L, used as the comparison series

The same constant L < 1 must bound all sufficiently late ratios; merely having each ratio < 1 is not enough.

Why \lvert a_n\rvert \le \lvert a_N\rvert L^{n-N}, and why isn't "each ratio < 1" enough?

Multiply the ratio bounds: \lvert a_{N+k}\rvert = \lvert a_N\rvert \cdot \frac{\lvert a_{N+1}\rvert}{\lvert a_N\rvert} \cdots \frac{\lvert a_{N+k}\rvert}{\lvert a_{N+k-1}\rvert} \le \lvert a_N\rvert L^k. The right side is a convergent geometric series (0 \le L < 1), so \sum \lvert a_n\rvert converges by comparison. Without a fixed L: the harmonic series has ratios \frac{n}{n+1} < 1 for every n, yet diverges — the ratios creep up to 1, so no single L < 1 bounds them all.

Ratio test: the limit form

Suppose a_n \neq 0 for all sufficiently large n and the (possibly infinite) limit exists:

L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert.
  • If L < 1, then \sum a_n converges absolutely.
  • If L > 1 (including L = +\infty), then \sum a_n diverges.
  • If L = 1, the test gives no conclusion.
Symbols
  • L \in [0, +\infty] — the limit of the ratio sizes (it can be +\infty)

When L < 1, the ratios are eventually bounded by a fixed number below 1. When L > 1, the ratios are eventually at least 1.

Worked example — the ratio test, both forms

(a) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n^2}{3^n}.

  1. Form the ratio: \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(n+1)^2}{3^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{3^n}{n^2} = \frac13\left(1 + \frac1n\right)^2.
  2. Limit: L = \frac13 < 1, so the series converges absolutely. (Geometric-bound form: for n \ge 2 the ratio is \le \frac13 \cdot \frac94 = \frac34, so L = \frac34, N = 2 works.) (b) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n!}.
  3. Ratio: \frac{2^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \cdot \frac{n!}{2^n} = \frac{2}{n+1} \to 0 = L < 1: converges absolutely. (Factorials cancel nicely in ratios — the slide 49 rule of thumb.) (c) \sum \frac1n and \sum \frac1{n^2} both give L = 1: one diverges, one converges, which is why L = 1 decides nothing.
Connection

(b) is the series version of 7 Limits of Sequences › Factorials versus exponentials, which already used the ratio \frac{\lvert c\rvert}{n+1} to show \frac{c^n}{n!} \to 0. The ratio test gives more: \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} converges for every x \in \mathbb{R}. With x = 1 this is the factorial representation of e from 7 Limits of Sequences › Two more representations of e, and slide 51 names the general series: e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}.

Ratio test without a ratio limit

Consider the positive terms

a_n = \frac{2 + (-1)^n}{4^n}.

The successive ratios alternate:

\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \begin{cases} \frac34, & n \text{ odd}, \\ \frac1{12}, & n \text{ even}. \end{cases}
Symbols
  • 2 + (-1)^n — equals 1 for odd n and 3 for even n, so a_n = \frac1{4^n} (odd) or \frac3{4^n} (even)
  • odd n: \frac{3/4^{n+1}}{1/4^n} = \frac34; even n: \frac{1/4^{n+1}}{3/4^n} = \frac{1}{12}

Plot on the slide: the ratio values jump between 0.75 and about 0.08.

There is no ordinary limit. Nevertheless, \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \le \frac34 < 1 for every n. Hence \sum a_n converges absolutely.

Root test

Root test: a geometric bound

The n-th roots \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} give a second geometric comparison.

Absolute convergence. If there exist L < 1 and N such that

\sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} \le L \qquad (n \ge N),

then \sum a_n converges absolutely. Indeed, \lvert a_n\rvert \le L^n for n \ge N.

Divergence. If

\sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} \ge 1

for infinitely many n, then \sum a_n diverges. Indeed, \lvert a_n\rvert \ge 1 infinitely often, so a_n \not\to 0.

Symbols
  • \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} — the n-th root of the size of the n-th term: "which ratio L would a geometric series need to have this term at position n?"
  • L — a fixed number < 1; L^n — the geometric comparison terms (raise \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} \le L to the n-th power)

No ordinary limit is needed: a fixed geometric bound is enough.

Root test: limits and limsup

If the ordinary limit L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} exists, then:

  • L < 1: \sum a_n converges absolutely.
  • L > 1: \sum a_n diverges.
  • L = 1: the test gives no conclusion.

More general form. The same conclusions hold with

L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert}

in place of the ordinary limit. The limsup formulation also covers oscillating n-th roots.

Symbols
  • \limsup — the largest subsequential limit, the "eventual ceiling" (7 Limits of Sequences › Limit inferior and limit superior); it always exists in [0, +\infty]
Why does the limsup version work?

If \limsup \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} = L < 1, pick L' with L < L' < 1. The tail suprema u_N = \sup_{n \ge N}\sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} decrease to L, so from some N on they are < L': all late roots are \le L', and the geometric-bound form applies. If L > 1, there is a subsequence of roots tending to L > 1, so infinitely many roots are \ge 1, and the divergence form applies. The limsup is exactly the right quantity because it ignores finitely many terms and looks at the worst case among the rest.

Worked example — the root test

\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n.

  1. Spot the structure: the whole term is an n-th power (slide 49: "powers resembling c_n^n: root test").
  2. Take the root: \sqrt[n]{\lvert a_n\rvert} = \frac{n}{2n+1} \to \frac12.
  3. Conclude: L = \frac12 < 1, so the series converges absolutely. (Also directly: \frac{n}{2n+1} < \frac12 for every n, so \lvert a_n\rvert < \frac{1}{2^n}.) The ratio test would be painful here: \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} involves \left(\frac{n+1}{2n+3}\right)^{n+1}\left(\frac{2n+1}{n}\right)^n.

The root test can work when ratios do not converge

Let

a_n = \begin{cases} 4^{-n}, & n \text{ even}, \\ 2^{-n}, & n \text{ odd}, \end{cases} \qquad \sqrt[n]{a_n} = \begin{cases} \frac14, & n \text{ even}, \\ \frac12, & n \text{ odd}. \end{cases}
Symbols
  • a_n — positive terms that switch between two geometric sequences with ratios \frac14 and \frac12

The root values alternate, so their ordinary limit does not exist. Yet

\sqrt[n]{a_n} \le \frac12 < 1 \qquad \text{for every } n.
Symbols
  • \frac12 — a fixed geometric bound L; here also the \limsup of the roots

The geometric bound proves that \sum a_n converges absolutely.

The consecutive-term ratios also fail to converge: along odd n they tend to 0, along even n to +\infty.

Intuition — ratio vs root

Both tests ask "how does this series compare with a geometric one?" The ratio test looks at neighbouring terms, so it is upset by any irregular jumps (here the ratio is 8 at n = 4, larger than 1, although the series converges). The root test looks at each term on its own against L^n, so it is the stronger test. The ratio test is easier to compute when there are factorials. Both are useless when L = 1, which includes every series like \sum\frac{1}{n^p}.

From alternating signs to bounded partial sums

We have already seen two series with the same positive factor a_n = 1/n:

No cancellation: b_n = 1Cancellation: b_n = (-1)^{n-1}
B_N = \sum_{j=1}^N b_j = NB_N = \sum_{j=1}^N b_j \in \{0, 1\}
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1n diverges.\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n} converges.

Plot on the slide: B_N against N — one set of points grows linearly, the other stays at 0 and 1.

The next test extends this idea: even without alternating signs, bounded partial sums of (b_n) can help when a_n \downarrow 0.

Dirichlet's test

Theorem (Dirichlet's convergence test). Suppose (a_n) is non-increasing, a_n \ge 0, a_n \to 0, and the partial sums B_N = \sum_{n=1}^N b_n are bounded in absolute value:

\exists M > 0\ \ \forall N \in \mathbb{N} : \quad \lvert B_N\rvert \le M.

Then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n b_n converges.

Symbols
  • a_n \downarrow 0 — shorthand for "non-increasing and tending to 0"
  • b_n — any real numbers (e.g. signs or an oscillating factor); B_N — their partial sums
  • M — one bound for all partial sums B_N

We do not require b_n to alternate or tend to 0. We require the accumulated sums B_N to stay bounded.

Why does Dirichlet's test hold? (summation by parts)

Since b_n = B_n - B_{n-1} (with B_0 = 0), regrouping the finite sum gives summation by parts: \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n b_n = a_N B_N + \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} B_n (a_n - a_{n+1}) (checked numerically).

  • a_N B_N \to 0: bounded times infinitesimal (7 Limits of Sequences › Infinitesimal sequences).
  • The second sum converges absolutely: \lvert B_n (a_n - a_{n+1})\rvert \le M(a_n - a_{n+1}) (using a_n \ge a_{n+1}), and \sum (a_n - a_{n+1}) telescopes to a_1 - \lim a_n = a_1. So the partial sums of \sum a_n b_n converge. Leibniz's test is the special case b_n = (-1)^{n-1}, M = 1.

Dirichlet's test: a trigonometric series

Consider

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sin(n\alpha)}{n}, \qquad \alpha \in \mathbb{R}.

Take a_n = \frac1n \downarrow 0 and b_n = \sin(n\alpha). We need to bound B_N = \sum_{j=1}^N b_j. For \alpha \notin 2\pi\mathbb{Z}, the trigonometric identity

B_N = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sin(j\alpha) = \frac{\sin(N\alpha/2)\,\sin((N+1)\alpha/2)}{\sin(\alpha/2)}

gives \lvert B_N\rvert \le \frac{1}{\lvert \sin(\alpha/2)\rvert} for all N. If \alpha \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}, then B_N = 0 for all N.

Symbols
  • \alpha — a fixed real number (an angle in radians); 2\pi\mathbb{Z} = \{\dots, -2\pi, 0, 2\pi, \dots\} — the multiples of 2\pi, where \sin(\alpha/2) = 0 and every \sin(n\alpha) = 0
  • \frac{1}{\lvert\sin(\alpha/2)\rvert} — the bound M: the numerator is a product of two sines, so its size is at most 1

Thus \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sin(n\alpha)/n converges for every \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, by Dirichlet's test.

Where does the identity for \sum \sin(j\alpha) come from?

Multiply each term by 2\sin(\alpha/2) and use 2\sin x \sin y = \cos(x - y) - \cos(x + y) (5 Functions › Trigonometric functions): 2\sin(\alpha/2)\sin(j\alpha) = \cos\left((j - \tfrac12)\alpha\right) - \cos\left((j + \tfrac12)\alpha\right). Summed over j = 1, \dots, N this telescopes to \cos(\tfrac\alpha2) - \cos\left((N + \tfrac12)\alpha\right), and the same product formula backwards turns that into 2\sin(\tfrac{N\alpha}{2})\sin(\tfrac{(N+1)\alpha}{2}). Divide by 2\sin(\alpha/2) \neq 0. (Checked numerically for \alpha = 0.7, N = 1, \dots, 9.)

Intuition

\sin(n\alpha) keeps changing sign in an irregular pattern (unless \alpha is a multiple of \pi), but it never "drifts": positive and negative values balance out, so the running total stays in a band. Multiplying by slowly shrinking weights \frac1n turns that balance into convergence, just as for \pm 1 in Leibniz's test. Note the series does not converge absolutely for most \alpha, so comparison and ratio tests can't do this job.

Abel's test

Theorem (Abel's convergence test). Suppose \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n converges and (b_n) is a bounded monotone sequence of real numbers. Then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n b_n converges.

What the assumptions give:

  • The tails of the convergent series \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n become arbitrarily small.
  • A bounded monotone sequence (b_n) approaches a finite limit; its total change over a sufficiently late tail is small.

A proof combines these properties using summation by parts. Absolute convergence of \sum a_n is not required.

Intuition — Abel vs Dirichlet

The two tests split the work differently. Dirichlet: the b-part has bounded partial sums (but needn't converge), and the factor a_n must shrink monotonically to 0. Abel: the a-part already converges, and the factor b_n only needs to settle monotonically to some limit b. Quick way to see Abel: b_n = b + (b_n - b), so \sum a_n b_n = b\sum a_n + \sum a_n (b_n - b); the first converges by assumption, and the second is Dirichlet's test with the monotone null factor \lvert b_n - b\rvert (up to sign) and the bounded partial sums of \sum a_n.

Abel's test: an example

For n \ge 3, consider

\sum_{n=3}^{\infty} \frac{\sin(n\alpha)\cos(\pi/n)}{\ln\ln n}, \qquad \alpha \in \mathbb{R}.

First: \sum_{n=3}^\infty \frac{\sin(n\alpha)}{\ln\ln n} converges by Dirichlet's test, since \frac{1}{\ln\ln n} \downarrow 0. Next: \left(\cos(\pi/n)\right)_{n \ge 3} is bounded and non-decreasing.

Thus the original series converges by Abel's test.

Symbols
  • \ln\ln n = \ln(\ln n) — positive for n \ge 3 (\ln\ln 3 \approx 0.094), increasing to +\infty, so \frac{1}{\ln\ln n} decreases to 0; that is why the sum starts at n = 3
  • \cos(\pi/n) — \frac12, \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \dots for n = 3, 4, \dots, rising towards \cos 0 = 1: bounded between \frac12 and 1 and non-decreasing
  • Dirichlet is used with a_n = \frac{1}{\ln\ln n} and b_n = \sin(n\alpha) (bounded partial sums from the previous example); Abel then with the convergent \sum \frac{\sin(n\alpha)}{\ln\ln n} and the bounded monotone \cos(\pi/n)

Choosing a convergence test

Look at the terms

  • Non-negative terms: comparison or bounded partial sums.
  • Alternating signs, decreasing magnitudes: Leibniz.
  • Factorials or simple consecutive ratios: ratio test.

Look at the structure

  • Powers resembling c_n^n: root test.
  • Oscillating factor with bounded partial sums: Dirichlet.
  • Convergent series times a bounded monotone factor: Abel.

If the ratio or root limit equals 1, those tests do not decide convergence. No single test works for every series.

Worked example — a checklist in order

For a given \sum a_n, go through these steps and stop at the first one that decides:

  1. Term test: does a_n \to 0? If not → diverges.
  2. Known series: is it geometric, harmonic, \frac1{n^2}-like, or a constant multiple / finite change of one?
  3. Absolute convergence: study \sum\lvert a_n\rvert with comparison (polynomial-type terms), ratio (factorials, c^n) or root (n-th powers). Converges → converges absolutely.
  4. If \sum\lvert a_n\rvert diverges but there are signs: Leibniz (alternating, b_n \downarrow 0), Dirichlet (oscillating factor), Abel (convergent series × monotone bounded factor) → possibly converges conditionally. Example: \sum \frac{(-1)^n n}{n^2 + 1}. Step 1: terms \to 0. Step 3: \frac{n}{n^2+1} \ge \frac{1}{2n} for n \ge 1 (since 2n^2 \ge n^2 + 1), so \sum\lvert a_n\rvert diverges. Step 4: b_n = \frac{n}{n^2+1} decreases for n \ge 1 (as n + \frac1n increases) and \to 0 → converges conditionally by Leibniz.

An application: discounted rewards in AI

In reinforcement learning, rewards r_0, r_1, \dots are often combined into a discounted return

G = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \gamma^n r_n, \qquad 0 < \gamma < 1.

Suppose the rewards are bounded: \lvert r_n\rvert \le R for every n. Then

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \lvert \gamma^n r_n\rvert \le R \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \gamma^n = \frac{R}{1 - \gamma}.
Symbols
  • r_n — the reward at step n (any sign); R — a bound on all reward sizes
  • \gamma \in (0, 1) — the discount factor; \sum \gamma^n = \frac{1}{1-\gamma} — the geometric series
  • G — the discounted return (the slide-6 G_t with t = 0, up to the index shift noted there)

The discounted return converges absolutely.

Intuition

This is the comparison test for absolute convergence with the majorant R\gamma^n. Typical numbers: \gamma = 0.9, R = 1 gives \lvert G\rvert \le 10 — the agent effectively "sees" about \frac{1}{1-\gamma} = 10 steps ahead. With \gamma = 1 the bound disappears and the sum of rewards can diverge, like the robot's systematic error E_N = 0.01N on slide 6.

Key Facts

Partial sums and convergence

  • S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N a_n. A series converges if S_N \to S \in \mathbb{R}.
  • a_n \to 0 is necessary, not sufficient.

Non-negative series

  • a_n \ge 0 makes (S_N) non-decreasing.
  • Convergence \iff bounded above.
  • Compare with a known positive series.

Signs and absolute convergence

  • Leibniz: alternating, decreasing magnitudes \to 0.
  • \sum\lvert a_n\rvert < \infty implies \sum a_n converges.
  • Absolute convergence allows rearranging terms without changing the sum.

Other convergence tests

  • Ratio/root: < 1 absolute, > 1 divergent; = 1 inconclusive.
  • Dirichlet: bounded partial sums × factor \downarrow 0.
  • Abel: convergent series × bounded monotone factor.
